parts.title: Trait expression
paragraphs: Dominant and recessive describe an allele relationship for a particular phenotype. In a complete-dominance model, the heterozygote has the same scored phenotype as one homozygote. The allele associated with that phenotype is called dominant, while the other is recessive in this comparison. These terms do not specify which allele is more frequent, more useful or more recent in a population.

An allele can affect a product such as a protein or its expression. Sometimes one functional copy produces enough product for the scored phenotype, making a reduced-function allele recessive in that context. Other mechanisms produce other relationships. The visible dominance pattern therefore depends on what is measured; it is not a universal physical contest in which one allele erases the other.

Under a fictional A/a complete-dominance model, AA and Aa share the dominant phenotype while aa has the recessive phenotype. An observed dominant phenotype leaves two possible genotypes. A recessive phenotype identifies aa only under the stated model, including its assumptions about expression. Before using a cross or pedigree, define those assumptions and avoid transferring a classroom trait rule directly to a complex human characteristic.

parts.title: Genes and environment
paragraphs: A polygenic trait is influenced by variation at more than one gene locus. Many contributing variants can produce numerous possible genetic combinations. Together with environmental effects, these contributions can create continuous variation, where measurements spread across a range rather than falling into only a few distinct categories. Height is an example of a characteristic with many genetic and environmental influences.

Environment can affect development, gene expression and the measurement of a phenotype. Nutrition, temperature or other conditions can change how a genotype is expressed in an organism. A genetic influence and an environmental influence are not mutually exclusive explanations. To compare them, define a population, measured characteristic and relevant range of conditions rather than using one family resemblance as proof.

A heritability estimate describes how measured variation is associated with genetic differences within a particular studied population and environment. It does not assign a genetic percentage to one person's trait or show that change is impossible. Simple human examples such as tongue rolling, freckles or earlobe attachment should not be treated as reliable universal one-gene models. Use explicitly fictional traits when learning elementary inheritance rules.

parts.title: Controlled crosses and evidence
paragraphs: Mendelian inheritance models were developed from repeated, controlled crosses. The P generation is the parental generation chosen for a cross. F1 refers to its offspring, and F2 commonly refers to offspring produced by crossing or selfing F1 individuals. True-breeding lines produce a consistent scored trait under the breeding conditions used. This provides a useful starting point for testing how a trait is transmitted.

In a simple complete-dominance example, crossing two contrasting true-breeding lines produces heterozygous F1 offspring with one parental phenotype. Crossing the F1 can produce an F2 pattern close to three dominant-phenotype offspring for every one recessive-phenotype offspring in a large sample. The reappearance of the recessive phenotype supports discrete inherited factors rather than irreversible blending of parental contributions.

A reciprocal cross exchanges which parental sex contributes each phenotype. Comparing reciprocal results can test whether direction of inheritance matters. Record the actual sample sizes and observations before stating a rule. Agreement with an expected ratio supports a model under its assumptions; it does not prove that every alternative explanation is impossible. Controlled methods and repeatable observations make the inference stronger than a single small cross.

parts.title: Segregation
paragraphs: Segregation describes the separation of an individual's two alleles at a locus into different gametes. In an Aa individual, ordinary meiosis gives each gamete one of the two alleles. Under the simple model, A and a each have probability one-half. The chromosome mechanism connects this probability with separation of homologous chromosomes carrying corresponding loci during meiosis.

For an Aa × Aa cross, each parent can supply A or a. Combining these possibilities gives AA, Aa, aA and aa with equal basic probabilities. Aa and aA describe the same unphased genotype, so their probabilities add. The genotype prediction is one-quarter AA, one-half Aa and one-quarter aa. With complete dominance, the phenotype probabilities become three-quarters dominant and one-quarter recessive.

These are probabilities across possible outcomes, not a schedule for four offspring. Four dominant offspring can occur in a family-sized sample without violating segregation. Also distinguish segregation from independent assortment. Segregation concerns the two alleles at one locus. Independent assortment concerns combinations at different loci and requires suitable chromosome relationships. Evidence for one process does not automatically establish the other.

parts.title: Inheritance modes and notation
paragraphs: An autosomal locus lies on a chromosome other than a sex chromosome. In a simplified autosomal dominant model, one dominant allele is sufficient for the scored phenotype. In an autosomal recessive model, two recessive alleles are required for that phenotype. Define which phenotype the notation represents. The terms affected and unaffected in a fictional case are scoring labels, not complete descriptions of a person.

A Punnett square organizes gamete combinations. Write each parent's genotype first, derive the gametes and their probabilities, then place one parent's possibilities across the top and the other's along the side. Each cell combines one gamete from each parent. Add cells belonging to the same genotype or phenotype. If gamete probabilities differ, the square's cells cannot simply be counted as equally likely.

For Aa × aa, the first parent supplies A or a, while the second supplies only a. Expected offspring are one-half Aa and one-half aa. Under complete dominance, half have each scored phenotype. A useful answer includes parental genotypes, gametes, assumptions and interpretation. A bare ratio does not reveal which categories were counted or why the calculation applies.

parts.title: Probability and test crosses
paragraphs: A test cross pairs an individual with an uncertain dominant-phenotype genotype with a homozygous recessive tester. Under the simple A/a model, the unknown parent could be AA or Aa. The tester contributes only a. An aa offspring therefore demonstrates that the unknown parent supplied a, identifying that parent as heterozygous under the stated assumptions.

If every observed offspring has the dominant phenotype, the result is less decisive. An AA parent predicts that outcome, but an Aa parent can also produce an all-dominant small sample by chance. For an Aa × aa model, four dominant offspring in four independent trials have probability (1/2)⁴=1/16. Larger repeated samples can strengthen an inference without making an impossible claim about what a small sample proves.

An independent event has a probability unaffected by the other event being considered under the model. Earlier offspring do not use up future outcomes. If parental genotypes remain Aa and Aa, a previous recessive child does not change the next child's one-quarter recessive probability. Sample fluctuation is the difference between realized counts and model expectations. Distinguish that variation from evidence that a biological assumption failed.

parts.title: Monohybrid crosses
paragraphs: A monohybrid cross follows one locus. Begin by identifying the parental genotypes and the allele relationship. Derive the possible gametes rather than copying a remembered ratio. For Aa × Aa, each parent contributes A or a with equal probability. The four combinations yield a 1:2:1 genotype ratio. Complete dominance combines AA and Aa into the same phenotype, yielding a 3:1 phenotype ratio.

Other parental combinations give different predictions. AA × aa produces only Aa offspring, while Aa × aa produces equal Aa and aa probabilities. A genotype ratio and phenotype ratio answer different questions. If heterozygotes have a distinguishable phenotype, the phenotype categories may also follow 1:2:1 rather than 3:1. State the expression model before combining categories.

Use expected probabilities to evaluate observations. A small sample of ten from an Aa × Aa model has expected counts of 2.5 AA, 5 Aa and 2.5 aa. Fractional expected counts are legitimate because they describe averages over repeated samples, not fractions of an actual organism. Record actual whole-number observations separately and consider sample size before deciding whether a difference challenges the model.

parts.title: Probability rules
paragraphs: The product rule combines independent events that must occur together. If the probability of aa is one-quarter and an independent bb event also has probability one-quarter, the joint probability of aabb is one-sixteenth. State the independence assumption. Multiplying probabilities without checking whether one event changes the other can give an incorrect result.

The sum rule combines mutually exclusive alternatives. In an Aa × Aa cross, the two ways to obtain a heterozygote are A from the first parent with a from the second, or a from the first with A from the second. Each has probability one-quarter. Adding them gives one-half. Do not add overlapping categories without accounting for their overlap.

Conditional probability changes the comparison set when information is supplied. If an Aa × Aa child is known to be unaffected in a fully penetrant recessive model, remove the aa category. Among the remaining AA, Aa and aA possibilities, two are carriers. The carrier probability is therefore two-thirds. The unconditional one-half carrier probability applies before restricting the outcome to unaffected offspring.

parts.title: Dihybrid crosses
paragraphs: A dihybrid cross follows two loci. For independently assorting loci in an AaBb individual, A or a can combine with B or b. The four gamete types are AB, Ab, aB and ab, each with probability one-quarter under the model. Their independence can arise from independently orienting different homologous chromosome pairs during meiosis I.

In an AaBb × AaBb cross with complete dominance at both loci, the phenotype probabilities are 9/16 A_B_, 3/16 A_bb, 3/16 aaB_ and 1/16 aabb. The underscore means either allele can occupy that position while retaining the stated dominant phenotype. For example, A_ includes AA and Aa. A 16-cell square or separate single-locus probabilities can produce the same result when used consistently.

This prediction has conditions. Linked loci can be transmitted together more often than independence predicts, and other allele interactions can change the phenotype categories. A 9:3:3:1 ratio is therefore a model result, not a universal property of two-trait inheritance. In a test cross AaBb × aabb, equal gamete probabilities instead predict four equally likely offspring classes. Always connect the ratio to its parental cross and assumptions.

parts.title: Testing a model
paragraphs: An observed count is the result recorded in a sample. An expected count is the model probability multiplied by the sample size. To investigate an Aa × Aa model, first predict the 1:2:1 genotype pattern and specify how offspring will be classified. Keep parental genotypes, scoring rules and the inheritance model constant while comparing sample sizes.

The two small samples contain AA/Aa/aa counts of 3/5/2 and 1/7/2, compared with expectations of 2.5/5/2.5 in each ten-offspring sample. The larger samples contain 24/51/25 and 28/48/24, compared with 25/50/25 in each hundred-offspring sample. These are synthetic data for testing a reasoning process. Their larger-sample proportions are closer overall to the model, but increasing a sample does not guarantee every observed category moves closer each time.

Record the observations and expectations in separate columns. Explain a difference using sample fluctuation before claiming a new inheritance mechanism, then consider alternatives such as scoring error or differential survival. A stronger investigation repeats samples and checks the model's assumptions. Respond to the claim that any deviation disproves segregation by using the actual counts and probabilities. Revise your conclusion to state both the support and its limits.

parts.title: Incomplete dominance
paragraphs: Incomplete dominance describes a measured phenotype in which the heterozygote is intermediate between the two homozygotes. In a fictional flower model, RᴿRᴿ plants are red, RᵂRᵂ plants are white and RᴿRᵂ plants are pink. The superscripts distinguish alleles without suggesting that one must completely dominate the other. Define the notation before constructing the cross.

Crossing two pink heterozygotes gives one-quarter red homozygotes, one-half pink heterozygotes and one-quarter white homozygotes. The genotype and phenotype ratios are both 1:2:1 because all three genotypes are visibly distinct in this model. Each parent still segregates discrete alleles into gametes. The intermediate heterozygote phenotype does not mean the original alleles have blended into a new permanent allele.

The dominance relationship depends on the trait measured. A pigment concentration, a visible colour category and the presence of a particular protein are different observations. A useful explanation states the molecular or measured level and avoids treating intermediate appearance as the only possible allele interaction. Compare the predicted F2 categories with complete dominance, where two different genotypes can share one scored phenotype.

parts.title: Codominance and multiple alleles
paragraphs: Codominance occurs when both allele-associated products are detectable in the heterozygote. The simplified ABO blood-group model provides an example. Iᴬ and Iᴮ alleles support distinct surface antigens, while i does not produce those same functional antigen-modifying effects. IᴬIᴮ individuals display both A and B antigens rather than an intermediate blended antigen. The i allele is recessive to Iᴬ and Iᴮ in this model.

Multiple alleles means that more than two allele forms exist in the population at a locus. A typical diploid individual still carries only two of them at an autosomal locus. Crossing Iᴬi with Iᴮi produces IᴬIᴮ, Iᴬi, Iᴮi and ii with equal probabilities, corresponding to AB, A, B and O in the stated model. Write the gametes to show how each outcome arises.

Codominance and multiple alleles describe different features: expression within a genotype versus diversity of allele forms across a population. ABO evidence can exclude some proposed combinations in a closed classroom puzzle, but it cannot establish a unique person's identity or a certain relationship in the real world. Other evidence and model qualifications matter. Keep the exercise's inheritance assumptions separate from a medical or identity decision.

parts.title: Sex linkage
paragraphs: A sex-linked locus is located on a sex chromosome. In the typical XY model, an X-linked locus often has one copy in an XY individual, making that individual hemizygous at the locus. A recessive allele can therefore be expressed without a matching allele on the Y. An XX individual usually has two X-linked copies, so its genotype relationships differ from that one-copy case.

Morgan-type fruit-fly crosses helped connect inheritance with chromosome location. In a simple X-linked recessive eye-colour model, a white-eyed male crossed with a homozygous red-eyed female gives red-eyed F1 offspring. Crossing the F1 can produce white-eyed sons. Reversing the original parental phenotypes gives different predictions: a white-eyed female and red-eyed male produce red-eyed carrier daughters and white-eyed sons under the model.

A father passes his X to daughters and his Y to sons in the usual XY pattern. A Y-linked allele can therefore follow father-to-son transmission, while an autosomal allele can reach offspring of either sex through either parent. A trait seen only in males does not uniquely prove X linkage. Test alternatives, including Y linkage, sex-limited expression and chance in a small sample, using explicit genotypes and transmission evidence.

parts.title: Many genes and environment
paragraphs: When several loci contribute to a trait, the number of possible genotype combinations increases. A simple additive model can produce a range of outcomes as contributing allele counts change. Real traits can involve unequal effects and interactions, so the number of genes alone does not fix an exact phenotype. Environmental variation can further broaden or shift the measured distribution.

Compare a one-locus flower-colour model with a continuously varying characteristic such as body height. The flower model may fit a few categories under stated conditions. Height reflects many variants, developmental conditions and environmental inputs. A resemblance between relatives is consistent with shared genetic influences but also with shared environments. A strong study needs a design that distinguishes these contributions rather than treating one observed similarity as proof.

A claim that one established gene determines high intelligence is not a valid general model for a complex cognitive measurement. Genetic associations can be population-dependent and do not automatically establish a safe causal intervention. Evaluate the measurement, effect size, environmental context and independent validation. The purpose of studying simple inheritance is to learn how to test models, including recognizing when a simple model is unsuitable.

parts.title: Comparing model predictions
paragraphs: Different inheritance models can give different predictions for the same parental descriptions. A complete-dominance model can combine two genotypes into one phenotype. Incomplete dominance separates all three one-locus genotypes by an intermediate phenotype, while codominance detects both products in the heterozygote. Start with notation and the measured trait, then compare the predicted categories before examining the observations.

Survival can change the denominator of an observed sample. Suppose a fictional Aa × Aa cross produces AA, Aa and aa at conception in 1:2:1 probabilities, but AA is lethal before the offspring are counted. Among surviving offspring, the expected ratio is two Aa for each aa. This 2:1 result is conditional on survival; it does not mean meiosis changed its segregation rule.

Similarly, information such as sex, phenotype or survival can restrict a probability question. State which outcomes remain in the comparison set and then recalculate. A model must explain the scoring method as well as the inheritance mechanism. If an observation disagrees with a prediction, consider small-sample variation, classification, survival and linkage before inventing an unsupported allele relationship.

parts.title: Symbols and evidence
paragraphs: A pedigree is a diagram showing biological relationships and a scored characteristic across generations. A legend defines symbols, shading and any carrier markings. Generations are commonly labelled with Roman numerals and individuals with numbers within a generation. Relationship lines and offspring connections organize the observations. Read the legend before inferring a genotype from a symbol.

Affected and unaffected describe the characteristic being tracked under the exercise's definition. They are not labels for a person's overall health or abilities. An unshaded symbol ordinarily records a phenotype, not necessarily a known non-carrier genotype. If the source explicitly marks confirmed carriers, preserve that distinction. Do not silently replace unknown information with a certain genotype because the drawing looks simple.

Construct a fictional pedigree from a supplied relationship description before testing inheritance. Place individuals in the correct generations, connect parent and offspring relationships and record only observed or stipulated characteristics. Add inferred genotypes using symbols for alternatives where needed. This sequence separates the source evidence from the genetic model used to explain it and avoids importing personal family disclosures into the activity.

parts.title: Autosomal hypotheses
paragraphs: Under a fully penetrant autosomal recessive model, an affected individual is aa. Two unaffected parents with an affected child must each carry a, so they are Aa under the assumptions. An unaffected relative can still be AA or Aa unless the pedigree provides additional information. A carrier has a recessive allele without expressing the recessive phenotype in the stated model.

An autosomal dominant model gives different constraints. An unaffected individual is aa under complete penetrance, while an affected individual may be AA or Aa. An affected parent with an unaffected child must be able to supply a. A pattern appearing across several generations can support a dominant hypothesis, but pattern recognition alone is weaker than checking each required parent–offspring combination.

Keep alternative models visible until the data distinguish them. Penetrance, new mutations, small sample size and incomplete records can complicate real pedigrees. The classroom task should state when a simplified model excludes these possibilities. Assign possible genotypes rather than filling every symbol with a single unsupported answer. A hypothesis is useful when it explains the relationships and makes a prediction that another observation could test.

parts.title: Sex-linked hypotheses
paragraphs: For an X-linked recessive model, write alleles on the X chromosome explicitly. A carrier mother XᴬXᵃ and an unaffected father XᴬY can produce carrier or non-carrier daughters and affected or unaffected sons. Among sons, the affected probability is one-half. If the question also assumes equal probability of a son or daughter, the affected probability among all children is one-quarter.

An affected father's X passes to his daughters, while his Y passes to his sons in the usual XY model. A claimed direct father-to-son transfer of the same X-linked allele therefore conflicts with that transmission route. However, observing both an affected father and an affected son does not alone prove direct transfer: the son could have received an allele from his mother. Genotypes and family context are essential.

Compare X-linked, Y-linked and autosomal predictions across the whole fictional pedigree. A Y-linked model predicts transmission through the paternal Y line under its assumptions. A male-only pattern can also reflect expression differences or a small sample. State the alternative that remains possible and identify the relationship or molecular result that would distinguish it. Do not diagnose a real person's inheritance from a simplified diagram.

parts.title: Risk and information
paragraphs: Probability statements require a defined model and the information already known. In an Aa × Aa autosomal recessive cross, the unconditional carrier probability is one-half. If the child is known to be unaffected, the possible genotypes are restricted to AA or Aa. The conditional carrier probability becomes two-thirds. Explain the changed denominator so that a reader can see which question was answered.

Genetic information also raises questions about privacy, consent and access. Consider a fictional educational service that explains inherited risk using anonymous examples. A low-cost automatic report could reach more people, while a supported explanation could better communicate uncertainty. Evidence about accuracy addresses a scientific question. Decisions about privacy, fair access and acceptable uncertainty involve ethical and social judgments as well.

Evaluate social effects, cultural perspectives, environmental resource use, ethical obligations and economic costs explicitly. Compare the initial proposal with a perspective concerned about unwanted disclosure or unequal access, then revise the recommendation. The revised position should preserve scientific limits and state what is valued. A numerical genetic probability does not determine what a person should choose or justify collecting classmates' family information.

parts.title: Linkage and recombination
paragraphs: Linked loci are located on the same chromosome and can be transmitted together more often than independent assortment predicts. If one parental chromosome carries AB and its homologue carries ab, those combinations are the parental arrangements. Crossing over between the loci can produce Ab and aB recombinant chromatids. The terms parental and recombinant refer to the starting arrangement, not to which phenotype is more common everywhere.

A test cross can reveal the gamete combinations from a heterozygous parent when the tester's contribution is known. Under suitable conditions, an excess of parental classes supports linkage. In a model producing 40 AB, 40 ab, 10 Ab and 10 aB offspring, the two smaller classes are recombinant because of the stipulated starting arrangement. Counts alone require that arrangement or other evidence to identify the classes correctly.

Linkage is not all-or-nothing inheritance. Crossing over can separate linked combinations, and more distant loci can behave nearly independently in a two-point comparison. Scoring errors, different survival rates and small samples can also change observed class sizes. Check these possibilities before treating every unequal four-class ratio as proof of linkage. The best explanation connects chromosome arrangement with the observed combinations.

parts.title: Recombination frequency
paragraphs: Recombination frequency is the proportion of scored offspring that are recombinant in an appropriate cross. Add every recombinant class and divide by the total offspring across all classes. Multiply by 100 to express the result as a percentage. For 40, 40, 10 and 10 offspring in the stated parental/recombinant arrangement, the calculation is (10+10)/100×100=20%.

For relatively short distances, one percent recombination is used as an estimate of one map unit, also called a centimorgan. This is a genetic distance estimate based on observed exchange outcomes, not a direct measurement in DNA base pairs. It depends on identifying the recombinant classes correctly and on comparable detection and viability of the scored classes.

State the complete denominator and interpret the result. Ninety-two recombinants among one thousand total offspring gives 9.2%, not 92%. Excluding parental classes from the denominator would measure a different quantity. Sample variation means the observed percentage is an estimate. A good answer reports the conditional map interpretation and notes that undetected multiple crossovers can reduce the observed fraction relative to the underlying exchange events.

parts.title: Gene order
paragraphs: Pairwise distances can help infer the relative order of loci. Suppose the estimated distances are A–B=14, B–C=6 and A–C=20 map units. Because 14+6=20, B can lie between A and C in a simple short-distance map. Draw A–B–C with the intervals labelled. Reversing the entire drawing to C–B–A represents the same relative order.

Gene order and map orientation are different questions. Pairwise distances identify which locus is between the others in this example, but they do not establish which physical chromosome end must appear on the left of the page. Add a separate landmark if a fixed orientation is needed. Keep results from different crosses separate unless there is evidence that they describe the same loci and population.

Distances inferred from recombination are not always perfectly additive. Sampling and multiple crossovers can affect the estimates, particularly over longer intervals. More informative crosses can help identify hidden exchanges and refine order. Begin with the simplest order supported by the data, then state the limitation. A diagram should explain the calculation rather than merely presenting a memorized sequence of letters.

parts.title: Limits of linkage estimates
paragraphs: For two loci, independent assortment produces an expected recombinant proportion of one-half in the appropriate test cross. Loci on different chromosomes can show this pattern, and widely separated loci on one chromosome can also approach it because multiple exchanges reshuffle combinations. A result near 50% therefore cannot by itself distinguish those two physical arrangements.

An even number of exchanges between two markers can restore their original outer-marker combination. A two-point count may then classify the product as parental even though exchange occurred within the interval. This is why observed recombination can underestimate longer genetic distances. A sample proportion can fluctuate above 50%, but it should not be reported as a reliable two-point distance greater than that ceiling.

Check class assignment, sample size, survival and scoring before interpreting a borderline result. Forty-nine percent recombination is close to the independent expectation, but the precision depends on the number observed. Avoid claiming an exact physical position from a rounded percentage. A strong report distinguishes the measured count, the conditional genetic-distance estimate and the additional evidence needed to resolve a chromosome-location question.

parts.title: Evidence for hereditary material
paragraphs: Experiments helped distinguish which cellular material carries inherited information. In Griffith's bacterial work, live non-virulent bacteria could acquire a heritable virulent characteristic when mixed with heat-killed virulent bacteria. Transformation means a change associated with uptake of external genetic material. The result showed that material from the killed cells could alter the living lineage; it did not by itself identify the chemical responsible.

Avery and colleagues compared treatments that affected different molecular components of a transforming preparation. Destroying DNA removed transforming activity in their assay, while other treatments did not have the same effect. This supported DNA's role in the observed transformation. The inference depended on the treatments, controls and measured outcome, rather than simply on finding DNA somewhere in a cell.

Hershey and Chase used bacteriophages, viruses that infect bacteria, with different radioactive labels associated with DNA and protein. Their separation experiments found the DNA-associated label more closely connected with the infected-cell fraction and production process than most external protein material. Together, these studies constrained hereditary-material models in the systems tested. They did not independently establish every feature of DNA structure or every inheritance system in nature.

parts.title: Nucleotides and direction
paragraphs: A DNA nucleotide contains a phosphate group, the sugar deoxyribose and one of four bases: adenine, thymine, guanine or cytosine. The bases are abbreviated A, T, G and C. Nucleotides join into a strand through a sugar–phosphate backbone. Base order carries sequence information, while the backbone provides the repeated chemical structure connecting the units.

The sugar's carbon positions help define strand direction. The 5′ and 3′ labels identify different chemical ends, not left and right as permanent page positions. New DNA synthesis extends a strand at its 3′ end. A strand drawn left-to-right can therefore run either 5′→3′ or 3′→5′ depending on the labels. Always read those labels before writing a complement or predicting synthesis.

Separate sequence from orientation. For 5′-ATGC-3′, the aligned complementary strand is 3′-TACG-5′. If that complementary strand is rewritten in its own 5′→3′ direction, it becomes 5′-GCAT-3′. Complementing bases and reversing the display are different operations. A sequence without direction labels may be ambiguous for a molecular task, so state the assumption rather than silently inventing an orientation.

parts.title: Structural evidence
paragraphs: Chargaff's measurements showed relationships among base amounts in double-stranded DNA, including approximate equality of A with T and G with C. Different organisms could have different overall base compositions while retaining these paired relationships. These observations constrained a structural model: arbitrary pairing would not naturally explain the repeated base-ratio pattern.

Rosalind Franklin's X-ray diffraction work provided important evidence about DNA's helical regularity and dimensions. X-ray diffraction records patterns produced as radiation interacts with ordered material; interpreting the pattern constrains a model rather than directly displaying a labelled molecular photograph. Maurice Wilkins and other researchers also contributed evidence. Credit the specific observations and measurements instead of attributing the entire discovery to one isolated image or person.

Watson and Crick used model-building to combine chemical relationships and available structural evidence into a double-helix proposal. A useful model had to fit dimensions, base pairing and chemical constraints together. It also suggested how complementary strands could support copying. Distinguish a model's explanatory prediction from later experimental tests of that prediction. Scientific accounts become stronger when several independent methods converge while leaving room for refinement.

parts.title: The double helix
paragraphs: The DNA double helix contains two complementary, antiparallel strands. Complementary means that A pairs with T and G pairs with C in the usual DNA model. Antiparallel means that the two backbones run in opposite chemical directions. If one strand is labelled 5′→3′ across the page, its aligned partner is labelled 3′→5′.

Hydrogen bonds connect complementary bases between strands, while covalent bonds form the sugar–phosphate backbone along each strand. These are different bond relationships. Separating the strands for copying primarily disrupts the interactions between them; it does not require cutting the backbone at every nucleotide. The external backbone and internal base arrangement help explain both molecular stability and access to sequence information.

Complementarity permits a strand to act as a template for another. Knowing one oriented sequence predicts its paired sequence under the model. This is the basis for reliable copying and for interpreting many molecular experiments. A diagram that shows both strands running in the same direction loses an essential constraint. Label the bases, backbones and ends, then test the drawing with a short written sequence.

parts.title: Semiconservative replication
paragraphs: Semiconservative replication means that each daughter DNA double helix contains one parental strand and one newly synthesized strand. The parental strands separate and act as templates. Complementary bases are added according to each template's sequence. The result preserves the information through paired copying rather than leaving one entirely old double helix alongside one entirely new double helix.

A comparison of replication models makes the prediction explicit. If starting DNA is labelled heavy and replication occurs using light material, the semiconservative model predicts hybrid molecules after one round. After a second round, it predicts both hybrid and entirely light molecules. A conservative model predicts separate heavy and light duplexes after the first round. The different distributions provide a way to test the models.

Meselson and Stahl's density-label experiments supported semiconservative replication in the tested bacterial system. The method measured the distribution of labelled DNA, not an animated view of every base being copied. Connect the observed bands with each model's predicted molecules. A result supporting one replication model does not mean that copying is perfectly error-free or that every organism uses identical accessory proteins.

parts.title: Enzymes and direction
paragraphs: Helicase helps unwind the DNA double helix by separating the paired strands. A primer provides an initial short nucleic-acid segment with an available 3′ end. DNA polymerase extends that end by adding complementary DNA nucleotides. The new strand grows 5′→3′ while the template is read in the opposite direction. These roles are distinct: opening the template does not itself provide the starting point needed by polymerase.

If a model shows open templates but no new DNA beginning at expected sites, missing or ineffective primers are one possible explanation. Other evidence is needed to distinguish that from a polymerase or substrate problem. Match each observation to the process directly measured. A visible replication opening is evidence of strand separation, not proof that synthesis has proceeded normally.

Describe enzyme actions precisely. Helicase does not cut the sugar–phosphate backbone into individual bases. Polymerase adds nucleotides to an existing strand end rather than constructing DNA 3′→5′. Primer removal and replacement must also be coordinated before the backbone is fully continuous. Using a source–action–product sequence makes the mechanism clearer than listing enzyme names without explaining their order and dependence.

parts.title: Leading and lagging synthesis
paragraphs: A replication fork is the region where parental strands are separating and new strands are being made. Because the templates are antiparallel but polymerase extends only 5′→3′, the two new strands follow different patterns relative to fork movement. Leading-strand synthesis can proceed continuously toward the advancing fork on its template.

Lagging-strand synthesis proceeds in short stretches called Okazaki fragments. As more template becomes available, another primer allows synthesis of another fragment, still in the 5′→3′ direction. Each fragment grows away from the current fork region. The cell coordinates removal or processing of primers, replacement with appropriate DNA and joining of the remaining backbone breaks.

DNA ligase seals a backbone nick by forming the missing covalent linkage when appropriate adjacent ends are available. It does not invent a missing long sequence or choose complementary bases in place of polymerase. A model showing completed fragments with unsealed junctions points to a joining problem. Label both template directions and each new fragment's direction; the lagging strand is discontinuous, not chemically synthesized backward.

parts.title: Replication evidence
paragraphs: Replication models generate predictions about both molecules and measurements. A missing primer, a polymerase defect and a ligase defect can all reduce successful copying, but they predict different intermediate patterns. Open templates without new starts differ from many synthesized fragments with unsealed junctions. Compare these observations before choosing an explanation based only on a low overall DNA yield.

Proofreading is a process in which some polymerases detect and correct certain mismatches during synthesis. Other repair systems also contribute to DNA integrity. These mechanisms reduce error rates but do not guarantee perfect copying. A mutation is a lasting genetic change, and whether a replication error becomes one depends on correction, later copying and the cellular context.

If a proofreading-deficient model shows more mismatches, the evidence supports reduced copying accuracy under the tested conditions. It does not automatically identify an organism-level phenotype. The affected sequence, cell lineage, repair and expression all matter. State the measurement, explain the relevant enzyme role and name the next result needed to connect a molecular error with a functional outcome.

parts.title: Selecting a template
paragraphs: Transcription produces RNA using one DNA strand as a template. A promoter is a DNA region involved in positioning and regulating the transcription machinery. RNA polymerase reads the template strand 3′→5′ and synthesizes RNA 5′→3′. Which strand serves as the template depends on the gene's orientation and regulatory arrangement, rather than on a permanent label applying to an entire chromosome.

The coding strand has the same base order as the RNA for the region being transcribed, except that RNA uses U where DNA has T. The coding strand is therefore not the strand directly base-paired to the growing RNA. For coding DNA 5′-ATG GAA-3′, the aligned template is 3′-TAC CTT-5′ and the RNA is 5′-AUG GAA-3′.

Gene presence and gene activity are different observations. A gene's DNA sequence can be present while little transcript is produced because initiation or regulation differs. Conversely, abundant transcript does not prove abundant functional protein. Identify what the method measures and locate it in the DNA→RNA→protein relationship. Use both strand labels and direction before writing a sequence answer.

parts.title: Making RNA
paragraphs: RNA is a nucleic acid containing ribose sugar and the bases A, U, G and C. Uracil, abbreviated U, pairs with A in the relevant transcription relationship. RNA polymerase builds a complementary RNA strand as it follows the DNA template. The growing transcript is synthesized 5′→3′ and separates from the template as transcription progresses.

Given template DNA 3′-TAC CTT AAA ATT-5′, complementary RNA is 5′-AUG GAA UUU UAA-3′. Read each paired base and retain the opposite directions. If the supplied template is instead written 5′→3′, reverse the displayed order before expressing the resulting RNA in its own 5′→3′ direction. A direction label changes the task; it is not decorative punctuation.

Transcription produces an RNA molecule rather than directly assembling amino acids. Some RNAs carry a message used in translation, while others have structural or functional roles. In a sequence task, identify whether the source gives coding DNA, template DNA or RNA before applying base-pair rules. An answer that complements the coding strand and calls that product mRNA has confused the two DNA roles.

parts.title: Processing and expression
paragraphs: A primary RNA transcript is the initial product made from a gene. In many eukaryotic protein-coding genes, it contains regions that will be treated differently during processing. Introns are removed from the transcript, while exons are retained and joined through splicing. An exon is a retained segment; not every nucleotide within an exon must encode an amino acid.

Processed messenger RNA, or mRNA, can carry the information used for protein synthesis. Additional processing, including end modifications, supports handling and function of many eukaryotic messages. Different splicing patterns can sometimes produce distinct mature transcripts from the same gene region. For example, two messages may share exons 1 and 3 while differing in whether exon 2 is retained.

Different tissues generally share the same inherited genome but use different genes and processing patterns. Brain and liver cells can therefore function differently without requiring entirely different inherited chromosome sets. Somatic mutations and other cell-lineage differences can qualify a claim of exact sequence identity. A comparison should distinguish DNA presence, transcript form and protein abundance, since each measurement addresses a different step in expression.
parts.status: authored-core-prose-initial-science-review; figure/worked/check/advanced and exact-source second review pending

parts.title: Checking a sequence claim
paragraphs: A correct sequence answer must identify the molecule, strand role, direction and reading assumption. Suppose a source explicitly gives coding DNA 5′-TAC ACA TGC ATC-3′. Its corresponding RNA is 5′-UAC ACA UGC AUC-3′ for that region. Do not reinterpret the stated coding strand as a template just because its first triplet resembles a familiar classroom example.

If that RNA segment is translated from the stated first-base frame, it specifies Tyr–Thr–Cys–Ile. The fragment does not establish a complete initiation context. An internal triplet only functions as a codon within an identified frame and translated region. State an assumption when the question supplies a fragment without enough biological context; a missing label cannot be repaired by pretending the source was unambiguous.

Sequence and abundance also answer different questions. A correct RNA sequence prediction does not show how much transcript a cell produces. Low RNA abundance can reflect altered production or stability, while low protein despite abundant RNA points to later steps as possibilities. Compare the methods and intermediate evidence. A strong molecular explanation follows the specific claim through direction, pairing, expression and the limits of the observation.

parts.title: Reading the genetic code
paragraphs: A codon is a three-base sequence in mRNA read within a specified frame. The standard genetic code relates codons to amino acids or a termination signal. Read the mRNA 5′→3′ and divide it into triplets from the stated start. A reading frame identifies which bases belong to each triplet; shifting that grouping changes the codons even when the underlying letters are unchanged.

AUG commonly serves as the start codon and codes for methionine in the standard table used here. UAA, UAG and UGA are stop codons. They signal termination rather than adding an amino acid called stop. Several different codons can specify the same amino acid, so some base substitutions leave the amino-acid sequence unchanged. The code table must be read using RNA bases, including U rather than T.

For mRNA 5′-AUG GAA UUU UAA-3′ in the indicated frame, translation produces Met–Glu–Phe followed by termination. Do not continue into later triplets after that stop when interpreting this open reading frame. A short sequence fragment without an initiation context requires a stated frame assumption. The presence of the letters AUG somewhere in a fragment does not by itself establish that a cell initiates translation there.
parts.status: authored-core-prose-initial-science-review; figure/worked/check/advanced and exact-source second review pending

parts.title: Adaptors and peptide bonds
paragraphs: Transfer RNA, or tRNA, acts as an adaptor between an mRNA codon and an amino acid. A tRNA carries an anticodon that can pair with a corresponding codon and is attached to an appropriate amino acid by cellular enzymes. The mRNA supplies the codon being read; the tRNA supplies the anticodon. These names identify different molecules and should not be exchanged in a diagram.

Pairing is antiparallel. The codon 5′-GAA-3′ can align with an anticodon written 3′-CUU-5′, or equivalently 5′-UUC-3′ when written in the opposite display direction. This pairing supports delivery of glutamate in the standard code. Direction labels explain why two differently written anticodon strings can represent the same oriented sequence.

The ribosome organizes the message and tRNAs and supports peptide-bond formation. A peptide bond links amino acids into a growing polypeptide chain. Ribosomal RNA, or rRNA, has structural and catalytic roles within the ribosome. mRNA, tRNA and rRNA therefore contribute distinct functions to one process. Pairing alone does not make the whole protein; correct amino-acid loading, ribosome activity and ordered movement are also required.

parts.title: Initiation to termination
paragraphs: Initiation establishes the translation machinery at an appropriate start region and fixes the reading frame. The mRNA, ribosomal subunits and an initiating tRNA assemble in a coordinated way. Once the start frame is established, the ribosome progresses through successive codons. The same message can be used repeatedly, allowing more than one polypeptide molecule to be produced from its information.

During elongation, a suitable charged tRNA enters, its anticodon pairs with the next codon and the growing chain is transferred through peptide-bond formation. The ribosome moves along the mRNA so that the next codon can be read. The sequence of codons therefore helps determine the order of amino acids rather than merely the overall number of each amino-acid type.

When a stop codon enters the decoding region, a release factor supports termination and release of the chain. There is no ordinary amino-acid-carrying tRNA that adds a stop amino acid at that point. The completed chain can then fold and undergo further processing. Sequence prediction describes the immediate chain under the stated code and frame; it does not by itself prove that a mature functional protein accumulates in a cell.

parts.title: From sequence to function
paragraphs: A polypeptide is a chain of amino acids linked by peptide bonds. Its sequence influences how it folds and interacts with other molecules. Amino acids differ in properties such as charge, size and interactions with water. A change at one position can therefore have a different effect from the same type of change at another position, depending on the protein's structure and role.

Folding produces a three-dimensional arrangement that helps determine function. Some proteins also require processing, partner molecules or assembly with other chains. A correct coding sequence is one part of the pathway. Transcription, RNA handling, translation, folding and stability all influence how much functional product is available. Low protein abundance does not uniquely establish a DNA deletion or a transcription defect.

A missense change replaces one encoded amino acid with another. Its effect may be small, substantial or undetected under the conditions measured. Compare sequence evidence with protein amount, activity and cellular response before inferring a phenotype. The most useful explanation identifies the immediate predicted change and the next experiment needed to test its consequence, rather than treating any amino-acid difference as automatically harmful.

parts.title: Types of sequence change
paragraphs: A substitution replaces one nucleotide with another. An insertion adds nucleotide sequence, while a deletion removes sequence. The effect depends on where the change occurs and which biological process uses that region. A change within a protein-coding region must be interpreted relative to a stated reading frame. Changes in regulatory or RNA-processing regions require a different kind of prediction.

An insertion or deletion whose length is not a multiple of three can shift the downstream reading frame within a coding region. This frameshift changes how later bases are grouped into codons and may alter later amino acids or stop placement. A three-base insertion preserves the downstream frame, although it can add amino-acid information and affect a codon at the insertion boundary.

Write the original and changed sequence with aligned positions before translating. For coding DNA ATGGAATTTTAA, a single added A after ATG gives ATGAGAATTTTAA. In the first-base frame, the later triplets differ from the reference. This prediction assumes the segment lies in a translated region with the stated frame. A one-base change outside that region is not automatically a protein frameshift.

parts.title: Effects on gene products
paragraphs: A synonymous, or silent, substitution leaves the encoded amino acid unchanged in the stated frame. For example, RNA GAA and GAG both specify glutamate in the standard code. A missense substitution changes the amino acid, while a nonsense substitution creates a premature stop codon. These terms describe immediate coding consequences; they do not independently establish an organism's full phenotype.

A regulatory mutation can change when, where or how strongly a gene is expressed without changing its encoded amino-acid sequence. A change at a splice boundary can alter the mature transcript. Even a synonymous substitution may have RNA-related effects in some contexts. Therefore, no amino-acid change means no change to that predicted sequence, rather than proof of no possible biological effect anywhere.

Effects can be harmful, neutral or beneficial under particular conditions. Compare the changed sequence with RNA, protein and functional evidence. If the measurements show no difference under tested conditions, report no detected effect in that assay. If a shortened product is predicted, test whether it is produced and functional. The strength of the conclusion depends on the level of evidence, not simply on the mutation category.

parts.title: Inheritance and variation
paragraphs: A somatic mutation occurs in a body-cell lineage. It can be passed to daughter cells as that lineage divides, but a change confined to a somatic tissue ordinarily does not enter offspring through the germ line. A germ-line mutation occurs in cells contributing to gametes and may therefore be inherited by offspring. Identify the cell lineage before predicting transmission.

Mutation can create a new allele sequence. Recombination during meiosis instead rearranges existing sequence variants into new combinations, although errors associated with chromosome processes can also produce changes. These mechanisms contribute different kinds of variation. A new combination of parental alleles is not necessarily a newly created allele at each locus.

Mutations do not arise because an organism anticipates a needed trait. Their origin is not directed toward future usefulness. Selection can later change the representation of inherited variants when they affect reproductive contribution in an environment. A variant's frequency and a variant's origin are separate questions. This distinction becomes central in Unit D, where population change is evaluated using counts, inheritance and environmental evidence.
parts.status: authored-core-prose-initial-science-review; figure/worked/check/advanced and exact-source second review pending

parts.title: Evaluating mutation evidence
paragraphs: A mutagen is an agent that can increase the frequency of genetic changes under specified conditions. Dose, exposure route, duration, biological system and the measured endpoint all affect interpretation. A controlled comparison should include a reference condition and use the same detection method. An association between exposure and a change does not by itself identify the exact molecular mechanism.

Consider a variant found repeatedly in tumour samples. Recurrence alone can suggest a research question, but functional evidence strengthens a proposed role. If the variant changes a growth pathway in cells and reducing that activity changes growth in matched models, the observations converge on a possible mechanism. The result still has a scope: tumour context, other variants and model limitations matter.

Communicate evidence in layers: sequence change, RNA or protein effect, cell behaviour and broader outcome. Name uncertainty at each transition. A mutation presentation should include sources and types, specific sequence examples, effects, inheritance routes and a misconception correction. Use fictional sequences and supplied data for the classroom task. Neither an exposure model nor a tumour example provides a diagnosis or treatment decision for an individual.

parts.title: Cutting and joining DNA
paragraphs: Restriction enzymes recognize particular DNA sequences and cut the backbone at characteristic positions. A recognition site is the sequence pattern associated with an enzyme's action. Some cuts produce short single-stranded overhangs, called sticky ends, while others produce blunt ends. The resulting fragments depend on where the recognition sites occur in the original DNA, so the source sequence constrains the products.

Compatible sticky ends can pair through complementary bases, bringing fragments into an arrangement suitable for joining. DNA ligase then seals appropriate breaks in the sugar–phosphate backbone. Pairing and joining are different steps: base interactions align the ends, while ligase forms a covalent connection. Ligase does not invent the required base sequence or make every unrelated end immediately compatible.

For a recombinant-DNA plan, specify the DNA source, recognition sites, intended insert and receiving molecule. Predict the fragments before describing a successful construct. Cutting with a familiar enzyme name is not proof that the intended gene was isolated. A later sequence or fragment check is needed to confirm the product. The most useful diagram shows the original, the cut ends and the verified joined arrangement.

parts.title: Transforming cells
paragraphs: A vector is a DNA vehicle used to carry selected genetic material into a cell or maintain it there. A plasmid is a DNA molecule that can replicate separately from the main chromosome in a suitable host. A recombinant plasmid may contain an insert, a selectable feature and sequences needed for its intended expression. Each element serves a different purpose in the experimental design.

Transformation is uptake of external genetic material by a cell in the context used here. Uptake does not guarantee that every cell receives the intended construct or expresses the inserted gene. Selection identifies cells with a feature linked to survival or detection under specified conditions. A surviving colony can contain a vector without the desired insert, so selection must be followed by appropriate verification.

Check insert presence, orientation, sequence and expression separately. A failed insert-specific PCR result is consistent with an absent insert but can also reflect a failed assay; controls are needed. A plasmid's presence does not mean it necessarily integrated into the host chromosome. Some constructs remain separate, while stable integration requires its own mechanism and evidence. Trace each claim from uptake through persistence and expression before concluding that a cell's function changed as intended.
parts.status: authored-core-prose-initial-science-review; figure/worked/check/advanced and exact-source second review pending

parts.title: Amplifying and separating
paragraphs: PCR, the polymerase chain reaction, amplifies a selected DNA region using primers and repeated temperature cycles. Strand separation exposes templates, primers bind to suitable sites, and a heat-tolerant polymerase extends them. The primer positions help define which region is amplified. A positive signal therefore depends on both the target and the method's ability to amplify it under the chosen conditions.

Gel electrophoresis separates nucleic-acid fragments under an electric field. Under the standard comparison used here, smaller DNA fragments generally move farther through the gel than larger fragments. A ladder containing known fragment sizes helps estimate sample sizes. A band records a group of molecules with similar migration; it does not independently reveal every base in those molecules.

Use a negative control to check contamination or background amplification and a known positive control to check whether the method can produce the expected signal. A band in the negative control weakens the interpretation of sample bands. Resolution also matters: fragments differing by one base may not separate clearly in an ordinary gel. Report the size evidence and its limits before claiming a specific sequence change or identity.
parts.status: authored-core-prose-initial-science-review; figure/worked/check/advanced and exact-source second review pending

parts.title: Genetic evidence and relatedness
paragraphs: Relatedness can be investigated by comparing aligned homologous DNA sequences. Alignment places corresponding positions together so that similarities and differences refer to comparable regions. A greater similarity can support closer relationship under an appropriate evolutionary model, but the conclusion depends on the region, mutation patterns, sampling and alternative explanations. A short matching sequence does not establish complete genomic identity.

Nuclear DNA represents chromosome contributions from both parents in the usual sexual model. Mitochondrial DNA follows predominantly maternal inheritance in humans and many other animals. Chloroplast DNA comes from a plant organelle and can have species-specific inheritance patterns, often uniparental. These sources can therefore record different histories. State which DNA was sampled instead of treating all sequence comparisons as interchangeable.

Keep sequence evidence distinct from fragment-size evidence. In the supplied molecular investigation, the displayed short coding segment is only part of a larger model region. Separate fragment measurements are 400+600 bases for reference and substitution, and 401+600 for an insertion model. The one-base size difference may be unresolved on an ordinary gel. Compare oriented sequences to distinguish the specific changes, then use the fragment data as separate supporting evidence rather than deriving full fragment lengths from a short excerpt.

parts.title: Applications and uncertainty
paragraphs: Genetic technologies can support research, testing, conservation, agriculture and attempts to alter gene function. Gene therapy aims to change genetic function in a treatment context, while genetic testing measures selected features for a defined question. A successful molecular step does not guarantee a complete intended outcome. Uptake, expression, function, delivery and broader effects each need appropriate evidence.

Technologies can have intended and unintended consequences for people and the environment. A crop construct may support one farming goal while raising questions about ecological effects, access, cost or movement of genetic material. Evidence of a matching sequence in another plant does not prove one transfer route or reproductive compatibility. Research supporting a sustainable society, economy and environment must compare benefits, uncertainties and the conditions of use.

For the supplied investigation, predict how a substitution and an insertion would affect the displayed coding segment and separate fragment measurements. Record sequence and size evidence, compare their resolution and explain which result distinguishes the models. Propose controls and a further test, then revise the claim that matching bands prove identical DNA. In a fictional technology decision, also consider privacy, consent, equity and a contrasting stakeholder perspective. A defensible recommendation identifies both the evidence-supported capability and the unresolved consequence.

parts.title: Populations and allele counts
paragraphs: A population is a defined group of organisms of one species in a stated place and time. Its gene pool contains the allele copies carried by its members. A genotype describes an individual's allele combination at the locus being studied. Population genetics compares these copies across many individuals, so the population boundary and the counted locus must be clear before a frequency is calculated.

At a two-allele autosomal locus in diploid organisms, each individual contributes two allele copies. An AA individual contributes two A copies, an Aa individual contributes one A and one a, and an aa individual contributes two a copies. For N individuals, the denominator is 2N. Count copies rather than simply counting how many organisms show the dominant phenotype.

In a sample of 100 with 36 AA, 48 Aa and 16 aa individuals, there are 120 A copies and 80 a copies among 200 total. The allele frequencies are therefore 0.60 and 0.40. This calculation uses observed genotypes and does not require equilibrium. State the sample and denominator; an allele fraction in one sampled population is not automatically a value for the whole species.

parts.title: Allele and genotype frequencies
paragraphs: For a two-allele locus, let p represent the frequency of A and q the frequency of a. Because those are the only allele categories in the model, p+q=1. This equation counts alleles. The genotype-frequency equation p²+2pq+q²=1 describes expected genotype combinations under the Hardy–Weinberg model, where gamete contributions combine randomly under the stated assumptions.

The product p×p gives the expected AA fraction, while q×q gives aa. A heterozygote can arise through A from one contribution and a from the other in two mutually exclusive arrangements, giving pq+qp=2pq. With p=0.60 and q=0.40, the expectations are 0.36 AA, 0.48 Aa and 0.16 aa. Multiplying by a population size of 100 gives expected counts of 36, 48 and 16.

Keep observed and expected categories separate. Observed genotype counts can be used directly to calculate allele frequencies even when the genotype proportions depart from the equilibrium prediction. The formula then supplies a comparison model, not a replacement for the observations. Check that allele frequencies sum to one and that predicted genotype frequencies also sum to one before interpreting a difference.

parts.title: Equilibrium assumptions
paragraphs: Hardy–Weinberg equilibrium is a reference model for allele-frequency stability and genotype expectations. Its usual conditions include a very large population, random mating at the locus, no mutation, no migration contributing different alleles and no selection among genotypes. These assumptions restrict the processes that can change the gene pool or alter the way alleles combine.

Large population size reduces random sampling effects. Random mating permits the p², 2pq and q² combination probabilities. No mutation excludes new allele changes, while no gene flow excludes reproductive movement changing the pool. No selection means that genotype differences do not produce different reproductive contributions in the model. Each assumption has a distinct role, so listing the five without explanation leaves the mechanism unclear.

Real populations rarely meet every condition perfectly. The model is useful because it provides an explicit expectation to compare with data. Agreement at one locus and one sampling time does not prove that all conditions were met or that the population has no other genetic change. A departure suggests checking the model, sampling and biology before identifying a specific cause.

parts.title: Solving and checking
paragraphs: If only a recessive phenotype is observed, estimating allele frequency requires extra assumptions. Under a fully expressed recessive inheritance model and Hardy–Weinberg expectations, the recessive phenotype fraction represents q². Take its square root to estimate q, then calculate p=1−q. Do not treat the phenotype fraction itself as the recessive allele fraction.

For a model with 9% recessive phenotype, q²=0.09, q=0.30 and p=0.70. Expected heterozygotes are 2pq=0.42, while expected dominant homozygotes are p²=0.49. The three genotype fractions sum to 0.49+0.42+0.09=1. To estimate counts, multiply each fraction by the stated population size and explain any rounding of an expected value.

Conditional questions require another denominator check. If the question asks for carriers among dominant-phenotype individuals, use 2pq/(p²+2pq), not the whole-population fraction 2pq. The same numerical data can therefore answer different questions. State the inheritance and equilibrium assumptions, show the intermediate calculation and label whether the result is an allele frequency, genotype frequency, conditional fraction or expected count.

parts.title: A model and its limits
paragraphs: A model separates what is observed from what is expected under assumptions. In the supplied gene-pool dataset, the initial AA/Aa/aa counts are 36/48/16, giving p=0.60. The middle observation is 45/45/10, giving p=0.675. The later sample is 42/46/12, giving p=0.65. Each row contains 100 diploid individuals, so the denominator remains 200 allele copies.

These changes show that the observed allele proportions differ across the samples. The middle row is labelled after movement, which provides context, but the counts alone do not isolate movement from every other influence. Sampling, selection or other events could also contribute. Compare observed genotype proportions with the equilibrium expectation calculated from each row's own allele frequency, rather than reusing the initial p for every row.

Plan the investigation by predicting what additional evidence would distinguish gene flow from drift or selection. Record counts, copy totals and frequencies with consistent notation. Explain the pattern, consider an alternative and revise a claim that one changed p identifies one cause. The model can predict future observations under stated conditions, but its usefulness depends on testing those conditions. A fit is evidence about a defined comparison, not a certificate of permanent equilibrium.

parts.title: Mutation and selection
paragraphs: Mutation changes a genetic sequence and can create an allele that was not previously present in the population. Natural selection changes representation when inherited differences are associated with different reproductive contributions in an environment. Relative fitness describes reproductive contribution compared with that of other variants under those conditions. Creating a variant and increasing its frequency are different processes.

Suppose a bacterial sequence change reduces the effect of an antibiotic on a molecular target. If descendants carrying that change contribute more offspring during exposure, the allele can become more common. The useful effect is context-dependent: the same variant may have little advantage or a cost when exposure is absent. The mutation did not arise because the population anticipated the treatment.

Evidence for selection connects inherited variation with differential survival or reproduction. A frequency increase after an environmental change is consistent with selection but does not prove it by itself. Compare replicated populations, the affected trait, reproductive contribution and possible movement. A strong explanation identifies the sequence or phenotype difference, the environmental condition and the mechanism connecting that difference with later allele counts.

parts.title: Chance and population size
paragraphs: Genetic drift is random change in allele frequency caused by sampling between generations. Even if genotypes have equal expected reproductive success, the actual allele copies transmitted can differ by chance. The relative effect is often stronger in small populations. Independent small populations can therefore change in different directions under similar conditions, without each change representing an adaptive improvement.

A bottleneck is a sharp population reduction that leaves a small sample of the previous gene pool. A founder effect occurs when a small group establishes a new population with only part of the source variation. Both involve sampling. The surviving or founding group's allele frequencies can differ from the source, and some alleles may be missing simply because their carriers were not included.

Consider three isolated model populations starting at p=0.50 and later showing 0.10, 0.70 and 0.40. Divergent directions fit a drift explanation, particularly if sizes are small and conditions are matched. Selection or different environments remain alternatives unless tested. Record replicate sizes and conditions before assigning a cause. Drift does not consistently favour the allele that seems best suited to an environment.

parts.title: Movement and mating
paragraphs: Gene flow occurs when movement between populations produces a genetic contribution to the receiving population. Immigrants can introduce allele copies or change their relative frequencies when they reproduce. Emigration can remove copies from a defined population. Movement need not change a frequency if the incoming or outgoing contribution has the same allele distribution as the remaining pool.

Nonrandom mating changes how individuals combine their alleles through reproduction. Mating among relatives or similar genotypes can increase homozygosity relative to random-mating expectations. By itself, this rearrangement can change genotype frequencies without immediately changing allele frequencies. Distinguish a different combination of the same copies from the addition, loss or differential transmission of particular copies.

The population boundary determines the interpretation. A group moving into an existing breeding population can produce gene flow, while a small group establishing an isolated population can create a founder effect. The same general word migration is not enough to identify the genetic process. State where reproduction occurs, which copies enter or leave and whether the comparison concerns allele or genotype proportions.

parts.title: Resistance and evidence
paragraphs: Resistance is an inherited capacity to persist or reproduce under an agent that limits susceptible organisms. Antibiotic resistance concerns microbial lineages; herbicide resistance can concern plant lineages. Sequence changes or acquisition of existing genetic material can alter targets, transport or other cellular processes. The particular molecular mechanism requires evidence rather than being inferred from the word resistant alone.

Exposure can increase the reproductive contribution of resistant variants already present. Repeated use of one agent can therefore change population composition. This is selection acting on variation, not a population deciding which mutation to make. A comparison with unexposed populations helps test the explanation, while molecular measurements can identify how the variant changes the relevant biological process.

Technologies can bring intended benefits and unintended consequences. A fictional farm programme may improve short-term weed control while creating conditions that favour resistant weeds or affect other organisms. Compare crop outcomes, genetic evidence, ecological effects, costs and uncertainty. A revised programme should follow the evidence and define what will be monitored. This population model explains a mechanism; it does not prescribe an individual's medical treatment or a specific farm chemical regimen.

parts.title: Testing explanations
paragraphs: A time series records observations at several points. Repeated allele-frequency measurements can show a pattern, but explaining it requires comparisons that distinguish mechanisms. A control provides a reference condition, and a replicate repeats the comparison independently. Together, these features help separate a consistent environmental effect from random sampling or an isolated measurement problem.

To compare selection with drift, hold environmental conditions similar across model populations and record population size as well as allele counts. Consistent changes linked to genotype-specific reproductive contribution support selection. Divergent changes among small replicates can support drift. To test gene flow, also record movement and the allele composition of reproductive contributors. One frequency curve may fit several explanations if those observations are missing.

Communicate the strongest supported claim and its boundary. The statement an allele increased is an observation; selection caused the increase is an inference requiring additional evidence. Name an alternative and predict an observation that would favour it. Revising a model after new information is part of scientific reasoning, not a failure. Keep the original data visible so the revised explanation can be evaluated against the same evidence.

parts.title: Size and density
paragraphs: Population size is the number of individuals within a stated boundary. Density expresses that count per unit area or volume. For a two-dimensional habitat, Dp=N/A; for a three-dimensional sample, Dp=N/V. Units matter. Forty plants in five square metres gives eight plants per square metre, while forty organisms in five millilitres gives eight organisms per millilitre.

Distribution describes where organisms are located within the boundary. A uniform pattern is relatively evenly spaced, a clumped pattern concentrates individuals in patches, and a random pattern lacks the specified spatial structure at the scale examined. Resource patches, reproduction and interactions can influence these patterns. A species does not have one immutable distribution under every environmental condition or observation scale.

Converting density to an abundance estimate requires the habitat area or volume and a representative density. A density of six plants per square metre across 200 square metres predicts about 1,200 plants. If the sample came only from a dense patch, that extrapolation could be biased. Keep measured sample density, study-area size and inferred total abundance separate in both the calculation and the explanation.

parts.title: Sampling populations
paragraphs: A quadrat defines a known sample area in which organisms are counted. A transect follows a line or strip across a habitat, allowing comparison along a spatial gradient. Representative placement and consistent detection rules are essential. Convenience sampling can overrepresent accessible areas or unusually dense patches. State the population boundary, sampling method and what counts as an individual before collecting or interpreting numbers.

In the supplied data, five one-square-metre quadrats contain 2, 8, 4, 10 and 6 plants. The total is 30 plants in five square metres, giving a mean density of six per square metre. Multiplying by the 200-square-metre habitat gives an estimate of 1,200 plants. The variable counts show spatial differences, so repeated representative samples would help assess uncertainty.

Mark–recapture provides another model for mobile organisms. If 40 were marked first, 50 are caught later and 10 of those are marked, a simple estimate is 40×50/10=200. This assumes suitable mixing, retained marks, comparable capture probability and approximate population closure between samples. In the online investigation, evaluate the supplied observations and sampling design rather than handling organisms. Explain how changed detection or placement could alter an estimate without a true population change.
