parts.title: Four demographic processes
paragraphs: Natality adds individuals through births, while mortality removes them through deaths. Immigration adds individuals arriving across the boundary, and emigration removes those leaving it. Over a specified interval, population change is ΔN=(births+immigration)−(deaths+emigration). The final population equals the initial population plus that change. Use counts collected over the same boundary and interval.

For an initial N of 1,000, with 120 births, 30 immigrants, 70 deaths and 20 emigrants in ten days, ΔN=60 and final N=1,060. An open population can include all four processes. A closed-population model excludes immigration and emigration, but can still grow or decline through births and deaths. Closed does not mean constant in size.

Age structure can affect future demographic possibilities. A broad young-age distribution can support future population growth if survival and reproduction permit it, while other shapes imply different constraints. An age diagram alone does not determine future size because birth rates, mortality and movement can change. Historical diagrams require their date, scale and data source; an internally inconsistent percentage axis cannot support a precise forecast.

parts.title: Rates and denominators
paragraphs: An absolute growth rate divides population change by elapsed time: gr=ΔN/Δt. If a population increases by 60 individuals in ten days, its average absolute rate is six individuals per day. State the time unit and sign. A negative result describes a decline over the interval, while zero indicates no net change even if births, deaths and movement still occurred.

The curriculum's interval per-capita quantity is cgr=ΔN/N(initial). With an initial population of 1,000 and a change of 60, cgr=0.06 over the stated ten-day interval. This is a fractional change relative to the starting population. Dividing it by ten gives an average per-initial-individual measure per day, a different quantity that must be labelled explicitly.

Do not mix a decade fraction, an annual fraction and a per-day rate without converting the interval and stating the model. A fixed addition of ten individuals each year also differs from ten percent growth each year. The latter applies a proportion to a changing population and can compound. Always identify the numerator, denominator and time interval before interpreting a number as fast or slow growth.

parts.title: Exponential and logistic models
paragraphs: Biotic potential describes a population's capacity to increase under favourable conditions. An exponential model assumes a fixed proportional rate without changing resource limitation. In a discrete example with N=100 and a 30% increase per interval, the sequence is 100, 130, 169 and 219.7 expected individuals. The increments grow because the same proportion acts on an increasing population. A graph of size against time forms a J-shaped pattern.

Environmental resistance includes influences that limit realized growth, such as resource shortage, disease or other constraints. A logistic model represents growth slowing as population size approaches a carrying capacity, K, under specified conditions. The resulting size-versus-time curve is S-shaped in the simple model. Carrying capacity depends on the environment and resources; it is not necessarily one permanent number for a habitat.

Construct graphs with labelled time and population axes. Compare changes between intervals as well as the curve's overall shape. Fractional model outputs describe expected or continuous quantities and may require rounded interpretation for actual counts. Neither model guarantees real populations follow its exact path. Compare predictions with observations and explain whether changing limitation, disturbance or movement requires a revised model.

parts.title: Feedback and changing limits
paragraphs: A density-dependent effect changes in strength per individual as population density changes. Competition for limited food or contact-related disease transmission can become stronger at high density. A density-independent influence has an effect that does not depend on density in the stated comparison. Weather or a physical disturbance may provide an example, but its actual effects can still interact with local population conditions.

Feedback between abundance and resources can slow growth, but responses may be delayed. A time lag occurs when the effect follows the initiating change after an interval. If reproduction continues while a resource shortage develops, a population may overshoot a temporary support level and later decline. A delayed response can therefore create fluctuations rather than immediate stable regulation.

Classify the mechanism using the evidence, not only the factor's name. Drought can reduce water across a landscape, while crowding changes how that reduced supply is shared. A graph showing decline after a storm does not by itself establish logistic slowing. Compare repeated per-capita effects across densities and conditions. A useful explanation states which relationship was measured and how a lag or changing capacity alters the model's prediction.

parts.title: Life-history strategies
paragraphs: Life-history traits describe how organisms allocate resources across growth, survival and reproduction. Relevant dimensions include age at first reproduction, offspring number and size, reproductive frequency, parental investment and survival. Fecundity refers to reproductive output or potential under the stated definition. Increasing investment in one function can reduce resources available for another, creating a trade-off.

The historical r/K framework describes broad tendencies. An r-associated pattern emphasizes rapid increase, earlier reproduction and many relatively low-investment offspring in some conditions. A K-associated pattern emphasizes other combinations, such as later reproduction, fewer offspring and greater investment or survival in relatively persistent environments. These are comparative tendencies, not rigid categories that predict every trait of every species.

Evaluate an actual set of traits and conditions. Added adult mortality may be especially consequential for a late-maturing population that replaces adults slowly. A high-fecundity population can still be vulnerable if its required habitat disappears. Connect the proposed risk to demographic evidence rather than using an r or K label as a complete explanation. Habitat area, recruitment and survival all matter when predicting recovery.

parts.title: Interactions and their effects
paragraphs: Ecological relationships can be compared by their effects on both participants. In predation, a consumer gains resources by capturing and consuming prey, while the prey is harmed. Producer–consumer relationships include herbivores obtaining resources from plants or other producers. These effects can influence growth, survival and reproduction, linking an interaction to population change rather than merely assigning it a name.

Mutualism benefits both participants under the stated conditions. Commensalism benefits one while the other's measured effect is approximately neutral. Parasitism benefits a parasite while harming its host. A parasitoid develops in or on a host and ultimately kills it, a distinction relevant to some insect examples. Define what was measured and the scale before classifying a relationship.

Effects can change with context. A fungal partner may provide a plant with valuable nutrients in poor soil while imposing a larger relative carbon cost under other conditions. One species pair is therefore not guaranteed to have the same net effect everywhere. Compare benefits and costs for each participant using growth or reproductive evidence. A positive effect on one population alone is insufficient to identify the interaction's full category.

parts.title: Competition and defence
paragraphs: Intraspecific competition occurs among members of the same species, while interspecific competition occurs between species. Both involve overlapping use of a limiting resource. Reduced growth in a mixed group can fit competition, but total density and other conditions must be compared. A crowded mixed plot differs from a sparse single-species plot in more than species identity.

The supplied experiment compares five A plants, ten A plants and a mixed group of five A plus five B plants. Mean mass per A is 4.0, 3.0 and 2.4 grams, respectively. Comparing the two ten-plant groups helps control total starting density while changing composition. The result is consistent with a stronger effect of B on A in this model, but replication and resource evidence are needed to identify the mechanism.

Defences can alter biological encounters. Protective coloration can reduce detection; toxins can reduce consumption; behaviour can change exposure or access. In Batesian mimicry, a relatively undefended organism resembles a defended model, while Müllerian mimicry involves defended species sharing warning features. Such traits can have costs and do not provide complete protection. Heritable variants can become more common through selection; organisms do not intentionally evolve a needed defence.

parts.title: Population cycles
paragraphs: Population cycles are repeated changes in abundance over time. In a simplified predator–prey relationship, increased prey can support greater predator survival or reproduction. Predator numbers may then rise after a delay. Greater predation can contribute to a later prey decline, followed by reduced support for predators. This mechanism can create a lag between the peaks of the two populations.

A correlation describes a pattern of association. Two curves with offset peaks are consistent with a lagged relationship but do not prove predation caused the cycles. Food supply, weather, disease or movement can also affect both populations. Identify whether the data show abundance, a detection index or a harvest count, since different measures have different limits.

Compare the proposed mechanism with additional observations. Evidence of diet, survival, recruitment or a controlled change in predator access can help test a causal explanation. A useful graph labels species, time and measurement units and identifies the interval between peaks. Explain the sequence with a biological process, then state an alternative. Avoid treating one familiar pair of curves as a universal law for all predator–prey systems.

parts.title: Succession and disturbance
paragraphs: Succession is change in community composition following colonization or disturbance. Primary succession begins where developed soil and substantial biological legacies are absent, such as a newly exposed suitable surface. Secondary succession begins where soil or other legacies remain after disturbance. The distinction concerns starting conditions, rather than whether the change is natural, human-caused or always slow.

Early organisms can alter conditions through resource use, soil development, shading or other effects. These changes may facilitate or inhibit later populations. Different species arrive, grow and reproduce under the resulting conditions, changing the community. A forest fire that leaves soil commonly leads to secondary succession, but disturbance severity and remaining legacies must be examined rather than inferred from the event's name alone.

A climax community is a historically used term for relatively stable composition under particular conditions. It should not be treated as one inevitable permanent endpoint. Later disturbance, climate, species arrival and interactions can change the trajectory. A schematic showing rising biomass describes its drawn interval; it cannot establish unlimited growth. Compare actual composition, resources and history when explaining a succession case.

parts.title: Ecological decisions and communication
paragraphs: Ecological decisions connect mechanisms with desired outcomes and evidence. An indicator is a measurement used to track a relevant condition, such as recruitment, water quality or community composition. Monitoring repeats such measurements over time using consistent methods. A useful proposal states what should change, when it will be measured and which result would lead to revision.

Consider a fictional Canadian wetland restoration project. Research could test whether habitat changes improve recruitment while maintaining water quality and other ecological functions. Society may value access, cultural relationships and long-term environmental quality; economic evaluation considers cost and sustained livelihoods. Supporting research for a sustainable society, economy and environment therefore involves more than maximizing one population count.

Compare a proposal focused only on rapid abundance increase with one concerned about species composition and resource limits. Use demographic, ecological and genetic evidence where relevant, and distinguish a measured result from a stakeholder value. Revise the plan after considering the contrasting perspective. State uncertainty and an alternative explanation for any observed change. Independent digital analysis can demonstrate planning and communication without claiming that it certifies field sampling or live collaboration.
